title: Pointer Provenance in Rust vs C++
excerpt: Exploring pointer provenance, inspecting LLVM IR, and comparing C++ and Rust's approach.
content_html:
I’ve been exploring Rust, and one topic that got me intrigued is pointer provenance, particularly because it’s not easy to visualize.

To get a feel for vtables, what I wanted was to look at the actual memory, to see what it really looked like and prove that I could in fact call these functions through their respective function pointers. With provenance, I wanted to take it apart the same way, but it turns out it’s not so straightforward. This only got me more intrigued, so let’s see what we can find!

My first time hearing about provenance, I wondered, why hadn’t I heard about it before? It seems so crucial, yet a bit of an obscure concept.

What is Provenance: Pointers Are Not Just Glorified Ints

Let’s start by taking a good look at this snippet. It’s short, but our intuition can trick us if it’s our first time coming across this concept. void opaque(int*) is forward declared here, so for us it’s a black box. Neither we nor the compiler can rule out that this function dereferences p and writes to memory.

void opaque(int*);

int f(int* p) {
    int x = 1;
    opaque(p);
    return x;
}

If we compile this with -O2, Clang optimizes this to return 1. Let’s try this on Godbolt:

The question is, how does it know that int* p doesn’t point to the same memory address where x lives (meaning that opaque(p) could end up modifying x)?

The compiler assumes p can’t equal &x because p wasn’t derived from x.

When I first heard about this, I thought it was a bit of a strange concept. What does it mean that something is derived from something?

I mean, if pointers were just numbers (memory addresses), p could theoretically happen to hold the same memory address as x’s allocation on the stack. Good thing they’re not just numbers!

Let us follow the white rabbit.

This brings us to the core of provenance. That “derived from” relation is provenance: for every pointer, the compiler keeps track of which allocation it belongs to and may, therefore, touch.

I tried to find a way to print this mysterious provenance, but it turns out that it’s purely a compiler abstraction. It does not exist as an actual data field stored alongside the memory address. (There are exceptions though: feel free to look up the CHERI architecture to go down another rabbit hole).

Inspecting Provenance: LLVM IR

So what can we do to inspect it? If the compiler knows about it then it must exist somewhere. If so, there must be a way to see it.

This is how I learned about LLVM IR (intermediate representation), which is essentially a low-level programming language that acts as a bridge between high-level languages (like Rust, C++, etc) and machine code.

Let’s try it for this code instead, where we also pass &x to opaque to see what happens when the compiler doesn’t optimize that part away:

void opaque(int*);

int f(int* p) {
    int x = 1;
    opaque(p);
    opaque(&x);
    return x;
}

We can use the -emit-llvm flag on Godbolt to see the LLVM IR:


define dso_local noundef i32 @f(int*)(ptr noundef %0) local_unnamed_addr #0 !dbg !14 {
  %2 = alloca i32, align 4 // --> root of %2 allocation (x)
    #dbg_assign(i1 poison, !22, !DIExpression(), !23, ptr %2, !DIExpression(), !24)
    #dbg_value(ptr %0, !21, !DIExpression(), !24)
  call void @llvm.lifetime.start.p0(ptr nonnull %2) #3, !dbg !25
  store i32 1, ptr %2, align 4, !dbg !26
    #dbg_assign(i32 1, !22, !DIExpression(), !28, ptr %2, !DIExpression(), !24)
  tail call void @opaque(int*)(ptr noundef %0), !dbg !29
  call void @opaque(int*)(ptr noundef nonnull %2), !dbg !30
  %3 = load i32, ptr %2, align 4, !dbg !31
  call void @llvm.lifetime.end.p0(ptr nonnull %2) #3, !dbg !32
  ret i32 %3, !dbg !33
}

declare void @llvm.lifetime.start.p0(ptr captures(none)) #1

declare !dbg !34 void @opaque(int*)(ptr noundef) local_unnamed_addr #2

declare void @llvm.lifetime.end.p0(ptr captures(none)) #1

attributes #0 = { mustprogress uwtable "min-legal-vector-width"="0" "no-trapping-math"="true" "stack-protector-buffer-size"="8" "target-cpu"="x86-64" "target-features"="+cmov,+cx8,+fxsr,+mmx,+sse,+sse2,+x87" "tune-cpu"="generic" }
attributes #1 = { mustprogress nocallback nofree nosync nounwind willreturn memory(argmem: readwrite) }
attributes #2 = { "no-trapping-math"="true" "stack-protector-buffer-size"="8" "target-cpu"="x86-64" "target-features"="+cmov,+cx8,+fxsr,+mmx,+sse,+sse2,+x87" "tune-cpu"="generic" }
attributes #3 = { nounwind }

What the compiler does is to conceptually construct a DAG (directed acyclic graph), to answer the question of where a pointer comes from and whether two pointers can touch the same memory.

If the root origins don’t match, LLVM can guarantee that writing through %0 will never alter the value stored at %2.

100%

There is so much more to explore here that it’s hard not to get carried away because it’s truly fascinating. However, my original goal was to compare how C++ and Rust handle this, so let’s continue.

C++: What Happens If We Cast to an Integer?

If we were to cast &x to an integer, then LLVM must assume that anyone could rebuild a pointer to x from that integer.

#include <cstdint>

void g(std::uintptr_t);
void opaque(int*);

int f(int* p) {
    int x = 1;
    g(reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(&x)); // address of x is now 'exposed'
    opaque(p);
    return x;
}

The result is that the compiler gives up the optimization:

That’s a pity if we only wanted to read the address and never intended to cast it back to a pointer. Wouldn’t it be nice if we could communicate this intent to the compiler?

Rust: Making Your Intent Explicit

This is exactly what Rust provides with its powerful provenance APIs.

Inspecting Without Exposing

let p: *const u32 = &x;
let a: usize = p.addr();

p.addr() extracts the raw memory address integer while telling Rust’s abstract machine:

I am reading this numeric address for inspection, but I guarantee I WILL NOT cast it back to a valid pointer.

Provenance is therefore not exposed.

To mirror our previous experiments, we can try to see if the optimization was avoided or not:

What we see is that mov eax, dword ptr [rsp + 12] reloads x after opaque(p), meaning that, at least for now, the optimization is given up. Same as in the C++ case.

Still, we can benefit from using the more expressive API, and not relying on exposure semantics. It gives the compiler room to optimize in the future, and, by telling Miri explicitly what we mean, it can better help us catch bugs.

Preserving Provenance

In lock-free data structures, we sometimes need to store status flags in the lower unused bits of a pointer. It’s a very cool trick, which left me with my eyes wide open for a minute when I first read about it. I talk more about it in this post. Essentially, due to alignment, the lower bits of pointers are “wasted” (always 0), so we can use them to store flags.

What we can do is work with an intermediate pointer value, which will have the flag bit set BUT that also inherits provenance from the original pointer. This is exactly the functionality that with_addr provides us. After we’re done, we can recreate our valid initial pointer.

The tagged value is stays a pointer rather than ‘usize’ because an integer is just a number and can’t carry provenance.

let tagged: *const u32 = p.with_addr(p.addr() | 1);
// ...
let revived_ptr: *const u32 = tagged.with_addr(tagged.addr() & !1);

Keep in mind that tagged isn’t dereferenceable, given that p.addr() | 1 is misaligned for u32. Dereferencing it would be UB.

In short:

  • addr() reads the address without exposing provenance.

  • with_addr() builds a new pointer with a new address but the same provenance as the original.

Legacy Rust, Similar To C++

In legacy code, we’d have to do something like this:

let addr = p as usize;
let tagged_addr = addr | 1;
let revived_ptr = (tagged_addr & !1) as *const u32;
println!("*revived_ptr: {}", unsafe { *revived_ptr});

This code will run, but if we run it with Miri, it emits a warning:

warning: integer-to-pointer cast
 --> src/main.rs:6:22
  |
6 |     let revived_ptr = (tagged_addr & !1) as *const u32;
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ integer-to-pointer cast
  |
  = help: this program is using integer-to-pointer casts or (equivalently) `ptr::with_exposed_provenance`, which means that Miri might miss pointer bugs in this program
  = help: see https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ptr/fn.with_exposed_provenance.html for more details on that operation
  = help: to ensure that Miri does not miss bugs in your program, use Strict Provenance APIs (https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ptr/index.html#strict-provenance, https://crates.io/crates/sptr) instead
  = help: you can then set `MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-strict-provenance` to ensure you are not relying on `with_exposed_provenance` semantics
  = help: alternatively, `MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-permissive-provenance` disables this warning

*revived_ptr: 1
warning: 1 warning emitted

Actually, the reason that it runs is also interesting. What happens is similar to the C++ example. p as usize exposes the provenance of p, and since the reconstructed pointer points to the same allocation, provenance is recovered.

Provenance would be lost if we did some pointer arithmetic and landed in a different allocation.

Casting Without Exposing Provenance

To see what happens when provenance is not exposed, we can use ptr::without_provenance, which creates a bare address with no allocation behind it. (It’s useful for dangling or sentinel pointers, but it can’t be dereferenced).

let bare_ptr = std::ptr::without_provenance::<u32>(p.addr());
println!("*tagged_ptr: {}", unsafe { *bare_ptr});

As expected, Miri complains about a dangling pointer and tells us explicitly that it has no provenance.


error: Undefined Behavior: memory access failed: attempting to access 4 bytes, but got 0x20b28[noalloc] which is a dangling pointer (it has no provenance)
  --> src/main.rs:11:42
   |
11 |     println!("*tagged_ptr: {}", unsafe { *bare_ptr});
   |                                          ^^^^^^^^^ Undefined Behavior occurred here
   |
   = help: this indicates a bug in the program: it performed an invalid operation, and caused Undefined Behavior
   = help: see https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html for further information

note: some details are omitted, run with `MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-backtrace=full` for a verbose backtrace

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

Recap

Provenance, in short, is a hidden piece of information tracking “which allocation” a pointer originates from, which LLVM uses for optimizations.

In C++, uintptr_t casts force the optimizer to prepare for the worst case by disabling some optimizations.

In Rust, addr(), with_addr() and without_provenance() let you state your intent explicitly: you only want the number, or you are deriving a new pointer from an existing one. In principle, that gives the compiler room to optimize more aggressively. In our experiment, however, the Rust version is unoptimized too: x was still reloaded from the stack. Using more expressive APIs is still valuable though, as Miri can enforce the rules and catch bugs that stem from unintended usage.

I had planned to compare what Miri and ASan can catch, but I’ll save that for another post. It was enough new info as it is and it takes some time to fully wrap my head around it.

I’m currently between jobs and looking for a Rust role, so writing these posts keeps me motivated and has helped me find a sense of community. Thank you for reading, and I hope you enjoyed it!

content_html_zh:
I’ve been exploring Rust, and one topic that got me intrigued is pointer provenance, particularly because it’s not easy to visualize.

To get a feel for vtables, what I wanted was to look at the actual memory, to see what it really looked like and prove that I could in fact call these functions through their respective function pointers. With provenance, I wanted to take it apart the same way, but it turns out it’s not so straightforward. This only got me more intrigued, so let’s see what we can find!

My first time hearing about provenance, I wondered, why hadn’t I heard about it before? It seems so crucial, yet a bit of an obscure concept.

What is Provenance: Pointers Are Not Just Glorified Ints

Let’s start by taking a good look at this snippet. It’s short, but our intuition can trick us if it’s our first time coming across this concept. void opaque(int*) is forward declared here, so for us it’s a black box. Neither we nor the compiler can rule out that this function dereferences p and writes to memory.

void opaque(int*);

int f(int* p) {
    int x = 1;
    opaque(p);
    return x;
}

If we compile this with -O2, Clang optimizes this to return 1. Let’s try this on Godbolt:

The question is, how does it know that int* p doesn’t point to the same memory address where x lives (meaning that opaque(p) could end up modifying x)?

The compiler assumes p can’t equal &x because p wasn’t derived from x.

When I first heard about this, I thought it was a bit of a strange concept. What does it mean that something is derived from something?

I mean, if pointers were just numbers (memory addresses), p could theoretically happen to hold the same memory address as x’s allocation on the stack. Good thing they’re not just numbers!

Let us follow the white rabbit.

This brings us to the core of provenance. That “derived from” relation is provenance: for every pointer, the compiler keeps track of which allocation it belongs to and may, therefore, touch.

I tried to find a way to print this mysterious provenance, but it turns out that it’s purely a compiler abstraction. It does not exist as an actual data field stored alongside the memory address. (There are exceptions though: feel free to look up the CHERI architecture to go down another rabbit hole).

Inspecting Provenance: LLVM IR

So what can we do to inspect it? If the compiler knows about it then it must exist somewhere. If so, there must be a way to see it.

This is how I learned about LLVM IR (intermediate representation), which is essentially a low-level programming language that acts as a bridge between high-level languages (like Rust, C++, etc) and machine code.

Let’s try it for this code instead, where we also pass &x to opaque to see what happens when the compiler doesn’t optimize that part away:

void opaque(int*);

int f(int* p) {
    int x = 1;
    opaque(p);
    opaque(&x);
    return x;
}

We can use the -emit-llvm flag on Godbolt to see the LLVM IR:


define dso_local noundef i32 @f(int*)(ptr noundef %0) local_unnamed_addr #0 !dbg !14 {
  %2 = alloca i32, align 4 // --> root of %2 allocation (x)
    #dbg_assign(i1 poison, !22, !DIExpression(), !23, ptr %2, !DIExpression(), !24)
    #dbg_value(ptr %0, !21, !DIExpression(), !24)
  call void @llvm.lifetime.start.p0(ptr nonnull %2) #3, !dbg !25
  store i32 1, ptr %2, align 4, !dbg !26
    #dbg_assign(i32 1, !22, !DIExpression(), !28, ptr %2, !DIExpression(), !24)
  tail call void @opaque(int*)(ptr noundef %0), !dbg !29
  call void @opaque(int*)(ptr noundef nonnull %2), !dbg !30
  %3 = load i32, ptr %2, align 4, !dbg !31
  call void @llvm.lifetime.end.p0(ptr nonnull %2) #3, !dbg !32
  ret i32 %3, !dbg !33
}

declare void @llvm.lifetime.start.p0(ptr captures(none)) #1

declare !dbg !34 void @opaque(int*)(ptr noundef) local_unnamed_addr #2

declare void @llvm.lifetime.end.p0(ptr captures(none)) #1

attributes #0 = { mustprogress uwtable "min-legal-vector-width"="0" "no-trapping-math"="true" "stack-protector-buffer-size"="8" "target-cpu"="x86-64" "target-features"="+cmov,+cx8,+fxsr,+mmx,+sse,+sse2,+x87" "tune-cpu"="generic" }
attributes #1 = { mustprogress nocallback nofree nosync nounwind willreturn memory(argmem: readwrite) }
attributes #2 = { "no-trapping-math"="true" "stack-protector-buffer-size"="8" "target-cpu"="x86-64" "target-features"="+cmov,+cx8,+fxsr,+mmx,+sse,+sse2,+x87" "tune-cpu"="generic" }
attributes #3 = { nounwind }

What the compiler does is to conceptually construct a DAG (directed acyclic graph), to answer the question of where a pointer comes from and whether two pointers can touch the same memory.

If the root origins don’t match, LLVM can guarantee that writing through %0 will never alter the value stored at %2.

100%

There is so much more to explore here that it’s hard not to get carried away because it’s truly fascinating. However, my original goal was to compare how C++ and Rust handle this, so let’s continue.

C++: What Happens If We Cast to an Integer?

If we were to cast &x to an integer, then LLVM must assume that anyone could rebuild a pointer to x from that integer.

#include <cstdint>

void g(std::uintptr_t);
void opaque(int*);

int f(int* p) {
    int x = 1;
    g(reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(&x)); // address of x is now 'exposed'
    opaque(p);
    return x;
}

The result is that the compiler gives up the optimization:

That’s a pity if we only wanted to read the address and never intended to cast it back to a pointer. Wouldn’t it be nice if we could communicate this intent to the compiler?

Rust: Making Your Intent Explicit

This is exactly what Rust provides with its powerful provenance APIs.

Inspecting Without Exposing

let p: *const u32 = &x;
let a: usize = p.addr();

p.addr() extracts the raw memory address integer while telling Rust’s abstract machine:

I am reading this numeric address for inspection, but I guarantee I WILL NOT cast it back to a valid pointer.

Provenance is therefore not exposed.

To mirror our previous experiments, we can try to see if the optimization was avoided or not:

What we see is that mov eax, dword ptr [rsp + 12] reloads x after opaque(p), meaning that, at least for now, the optimization is given up. Same as in the C++ case.

Still, we can benefit from using the more expressive API, and not relying on exposure semantics. It gives the compiler room to optimize in the future, and, by telling Miri explicitly what we mean, it can better help us catch bugs.

Preserving Provenance

In lock-free data structures, we sometimes need to store status flags in the lower unused bits of a pointer. It’s a very cool trick, which left me with my eyes wide open for a minute when I first read about it. I talk more about it in this post. Essentially, due to alignment, the lower bits of pointers are “wasted” (always 0), so we can use them to store flags.

What we can do is work with an intermediate pointer value, which will have the flag bit set BUT that also inherits provenance from the original pointer. This is exactly the functionality that with_addr provides us. After we’re done, we can recreate our valid initial pointer.

The tagged value is stays a pointer rather than ‘usize’ because an integer is just a number and can’t carry provenance.

let tagged: *const u32 = p.with_addr(p.addr() | 1);
// ...
let revived_ptr: *const u32 = tagged.with_addr(tagged.addr() & !1);

Keep in mind that tagged isn’t dereferenceable, given that p.addr() | 1 is misaligned for u32. Dereferencing it would be UB.

简而言之：

  • addr() reads the address without exposing provenance.
  • with_addr() builds a new pointer with a new address but the same provenance as the original.

Legacy Rust, Similar To C++

In legacy code, we’d have to do something like this:

let addr = p as usize;
let tagged_addr = addr | 1;
let revived_ptr = (tagged_addr & !1) as *const u32;
println!("*revived_ptr: {}", unsafe { *revived_ptr});

This code will run, but if we run it with Miri, it emits a warning:

warning: integer-to-pointer cast
 --> src/main.rs:6:22
  |
6 |     let revived_ptr = (tagged_addr & !1) as *const u32;
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ integer-to-pointer cast
  |
  = help: this program is using integer-to-pointer casts or (equivalently) `ptr::with_exposed_provenance`, which means that Miri might miss pointer bugs in this program
  = help: see https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ptr/fn.with_exposed_provenance.html for more details on that operation
  = help: to ensure that Miri does not miss bugs in your program, use Strict Provenance APIs (https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ptr/index.html#strict-provenance, https://crates.io/crates/sptr) instead
  = help: you can then set `MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-strict-provenance` to ensure you are not relying on `with_exposed_provenance` semantics
  = help: alternatively, `MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-permissive-provenance` disables this warning

*revived_ptr: 1
warning: 1 warning emitted

Actually, the reason that it runs is also interesting. What happens is similar to the C++ example. p as usize exposes the provenance of p, and since the reconstructed pointer points to the same allocation, provenance is recovered.

Provenance would be lost if we did some pointer arithmetic and landed in a different allocation.

Casting Without Exposing Provenance

To see what happens when provenance is not exposed, we can use ptr::without_provenance, which creates a bare address with no allocation behind it. (It’s useful for dangling or sentinel pointers, but it can’t be dereferenced).

let bare_ptr = std::ptr::without_provenance::<u32>(p.addr());
println!("*tagged_ptr: {}", unsafe { *bare_ptr});

As expected, Miri complains about a dangling pointer and tells us explicitly that it has no provenance.


error: Undefined Behavior: memory access failed: attempting to access 4 bytes, but got 0x20b28[noalloc] which is a dangling pointer (it has no provenance)
  --> src/main.rs:11:42
   |
11 |     println!("*tagged_ptr: {}", unsafe { *bare_ptr});
   |                                          ^^^^^^^^^ Undefined Behavior occurred here
   |
   = help: this indicates a bug in the program: it performed an invalid operation, and caused Undefined Behavior
   = help: see https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html for further information

note: some details are omitted, run with `MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-backtrace=full` for a verbose backtrace

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

Recap

Provenance, in short, is a hidden piece of information tracking “which allocation” a pointer originates from, which LLVM uses for optimizations.

In C++, uintptr_t casts force the optimizer to prepare for the worst case by disabling some optimizations.

In Rust, addr(), with_addr() and without_provenance() let you state your intent explicitly: you only want the number, or you are deriving a new pointer from an existing one. In principle, that gives the compiler room to optimize more aggressively. In our experiment, however, the Rust version is unoptimized too: x was still reloaded from the stack. Using more expressive APIs is still valuable though, as Miri can enforce the rules and catch bugs that stem from unintended usage.

I had planned to compare what Miri and ASan can catch, but I’ll save that for another post. It was enough new info as it is and it takes some time to fully wrap my head around it.

I’m currently between jobs and looking for a Rust role, so writing these posts keeps me motivated and has helped me find a sense of community. Thank you for reading, and I hope you enjoyed it!
